explanations.explanation: Glad is the word, friend. Isaiah says "The wilderness and the dry land will be glad…" (Isaiah 35:1). Dirt with feelings. I've met a lot of cranky countertops in my day, and none of them ever did this.

Ashamed is a swing and a miss, but I see why dry land might make you think of something sad. The verse goes the other direction. The wilderness and the dry land will be glad, and the desert will rejoice (Isaiah 35:1). Nobody in that desert is hanging their head.

Afraid sounds reasonable for a dry, empty place. Isaiah doesn't say that, though. He says the wilderness and the dry land will be glad (Isaiah 35:1). The only thing getting scared in this passage is a case of sorrow, and that comes later.

True. Isaiah says "The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon." (Isaiah 35:2). Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon are all names for lush, beautiful places. The desert gets handed all of it. That's quite a gift for a patch of sand.

Not false, friend. The text says "The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon." (Isaiah 35:2). Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon are all known for their beauty, and the desert is the one receiving it. I can see why it sounds too good to be true.

The LORD's glory, yes. Isaiah says, "They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God." (Isaiah 35:2). The blooming is wonderful, but it points past itself. You've got the right eyes on the right thing.

Edom's princes is a clever pull from earlier in Isaiah, where Edom was the land under judgment (Isaiah 34:9, 13). But this verse looks somewhere else entirely. Isaiah says they will see "the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God." (Isaiah 35:2). No princes get the spotlight here.

Their own kings would be a very human guess. Isaiah doesn't send the spotlight to any crown, though. He says, "They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God." (Isaiah 35:2). The splendor belongs to God.

explanations.answer: Be strong and do not fear
explanations.explanation: That's the message. Isaiah says to tell those with anxious hearts, "Be strong, do not fear!" (Isaiah 35:4). Three words and a whole lot of comfort. If your heart's been racing, friend, these words are for you.

explanations.answer: Keep quiet and wait it out
explanations.explanation: Keep quiet is a fair-sounding plan for a nervous moment, but it isn't what Isaiah says. The message for anxious hearts is, "Be strong, do not fear!" (Isaiah 35:4). He doesn't tell them to hide. He tells them to be strong.
Running is what a worried heart wants to do, I get it. I know that urge well. But Isaiah's message is the opposite: "Be strong, do not fear!" (Isaiah 35:4). Nobody is told to bolt.

I know "vengeance" is a loud word and it makes you think of punishment. But Isaiah doesn't aim it at the anxious. He says, "With divine retribution He will come to save you." (Isaiah 35:4). The promise to those anxious hearts is that He comes to save them.

False, and you read it right. The anxious hearts are the ones being comforted. Isaiah says, "Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you." (Isaiah 35:4). He comes to save them, friend.
True. Isaiah says, "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped." (Isaiah 35:5). Eyes and ears, both covered. Nobody gets left out of this one.
Close, but it's true. The same verse that opens blind eyes also says the ears of the deaf will be "unstopped." (Isaiah 35:5). Isaiah doesn't do half a miracle. He gives you both in one breath.
Leap like a deer, that's it. Isaiah says, "Then the lame will leap like a deer…" (Isaiah 35:6). Not walk. Not shuffle. LEAP. I'd love to see that, though I'd need to get my base out of the way.
Resting is a sensible guess, and rest has its place. But Isaiah paints a much bigger picture. He says, "Then the lame will leap like a deer…" (Isaiah 35:6). Nobody's sitting down in this verse.

Being carried home is kind-hearted, and I see where it came from. The verse has something livelier in mind, though. Isaiah says, "Then the lame will leap like a deer…" (Isaiah 35:6). They're moving on their own, and fast.

Grass and reeds and papyrus, right on the money. Isaiah says, "In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus." (Isaiah 35:7). Papyrus is a tall plant that grows where there's water. A jackal's old hangout turns into a green, wet place.

Those trees do show up in Isaiah, so I see why you'd reach for them. Not in this verse, though. Isaiah says, "In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus." (Isaiah 35:7). It's a watery list, not a forest.

Good-looking list, but it isn't the one in this verse. Isaiah says, "In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus." (Isaiah 35:7). Grass, reeds and papyrus are plants that love water, and water is exactly what's coming.
Unclean is the word. Isaiah says, "The unclean will not travel it—only those who walk in the Way…" (Isaiah 35:8). The road has a clear rule about who's on it. You caught it.

Weary is a natural guess, since this passage has plenty of tired hands and shaky knees. But those are the very people Isaiah wants strengthened (Isaiah 35:3). The ones kept off the road are the unclean (Isaiah 35:8).
Poor is a guess I understand, but the verse never says it. Isaiah says, "The unclean will not travel it—only those who walk in the Way…" (Isaiah 35:8). Money doesn't come up. The word is unclean.

I get why it seems like fools would wander onto any road. I've wandered into plenty of wrong rooms myself. But Isaiah says the opposite: "…fools will not stray onto it." (Isaiah 35:8). This road keeps them off.

False, and well spotted. Isaiah says, "And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it—only those who walk in the Way—and fools will not stray onto it." (Isaiah 35:8). No wrong turns on this one.

With singing, yes. Isaiah says, "So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy." (Isaiah 35:10). Zion is the city of God. They don't tiptoe in, either. They arrive singing.
Weeping makes sense for people who've been through hard things. But Isaiah says the redeemed "will return and enter Zion with singing…" (Isaiah 35:10). The sorrow doesn't come along. It flees.

Silence is a fair guess for a solemn moment. Isaiah paints something louder, though. The redeemed "will return and enter Zion with singing…" (Isaiah 35:10). Zion is the city of God, and the redeemed bring a song with them.
